science.conclusion: Within the explicitly stated uniform, two-interface, approximately constant-force, quasistatic and reversible fixed-temperature model, the signs, factors, area change, energy distinction, boundary-direction rule and units are consistent.

checks.conclusion: F1 is explicitly the combined spring force and wire weight, not the spring alone. It excludes the film pull that it balances.

F is one surface's force; two equal forces add only under the same interface conditions and the illustrated common direction. A single interface is explicitly excluded from automatic doubling. Introducing this condition before the first equation would improve readability, not correct a missing scientific qualification.

Slow near-equilibrium extension, negligible friction/viscous loss, stable interface conditions and approximately constant force are stated. Downward F1 and displacement give positive A=F1h=2Fh; the upward film pull does negative work. Gravity is already included and explicitly must not be added again. This is not asserted for an arbitrary accelerating motion or varying force.

The textbook surface-energy notation is retained as a model quantity. The precise reversible fixed-temperature interpretation is surface free-energy increase, expressly not an unconditional whole-system internal-energy increase.

S1 is the initial one-face area; S2 is the final one-face area in context. Positive downward extension produces S2-S1=lh, so both faces give A=2 sigma lh. The retained U_{surface1}/U_{surface2} notation and registered correction are unchanged. Explicitly naming S2 and sigma earlier is a readability repair.

Approximately constant sigma is conditioned on stable temperature/composition and unchanged surrounding medium. The force-length statement is restricted to a uniform flat interface, and appendix liquid-air values are not generalized to a different medium.

Force lies in the surface tangent plane and is perpendicular to the local boundary direction. For curved surfaces the rule is local; differently directed boundary-segment forces are not summed as scalars. l is the one-surface contact length along AB, not the frame perimeter.
F=sigma l and J/m^2=N m/m^2=N/m retain the source relation and dimensional meaning. No numeric values or unit conversions were introduced.

findings.title: Give the opening a concrete experiment and plain mechanics vocabulary
evidence: To study the magnitude and direction of surface tension
findings.problem: The first sentence introduces magnitude, a movable boundary, vertical plane and little friction together. The next explanation relies on resultant, equilibrium and vector without defining them. An 8-year-old cannot tell whether resultant means spring plus weight or all forces, nor why a stationary wire has nonzero forces.
findings.localAction: Break the setup into short concrete sentences: upright frame, a thin layer of soapy liquid, wire AB sliding up/down, l its length. Give plain meanings beside first use: magnitude means size; perpendicular means at a right angle; equilibrium here means the wire stays still because forces balance; F1 combines the spring force and wire weight only. Explain that the arrow over F denotes a force with a direction. Retain the apparatus and every physics qualification.
findings.acceptance: Before the first balance equation, a reader can identify the film's pull, the two contributions to F1, and why they can balance without any individual force being zero.

findings.title: Define symbols before use and explain the final algebra step
evidence: The magnitude of the balancing external resultant is $F_1=2F$, and its work is:
It writes the final surface energy as $U_{\text{surface}2}=2\sigma S_2$.
This gives the relation between force and boundary length.
findings.problem: F is defined only after the first balance equation and intervening figures. A is never explicitly named as the amount of work. Sigma appears in the energy formula well before its definition at the end, and S2 is only inferred from the final-energy expression. The transition from 2Fh=2 sigma lh to F=sigma l omits the common-factor explanation.
findings.localAction: Briefly define one-face F and the equal-interface condition before the first -2F equation, without removing the later Figure70 explanation. Name A as work, meaning energy transferred by a force through a distance. Before the energy equations, explicitly name S1/S2 as one-face areas before/after and sigma as the surface tension coefficient, a force per unit contact length under the stated conditions. Name the retained U_surface symbols as the model's surface-energy amounts. At the final step, explain that both expressions describe the same work and the common nonzero factor 2h cancels for this extension.
findings.acceptance: Every equation symbol has a timely plain-language referent. The two-surface factor remains conditional, A retains combined-force work, and all retained formulas/notation remain unchanged.

findings.title: Explain the alternate wire view and second wire position in prose
evidence: Here, $\vec F$ is the force exerted on the wire by one of the film's two surfaces (Figure 70).
findings.problem: The existing TEXT inventory describes Figure70 as a circular wire cross-section and Figure69 as two wire positions, but the draft names neither change of view nor the dashed lower position. A child can mistake the circle for an extra bead/object or the two interfaces for two separate films. The movement h is not connected to the marked second position.
findings.localAction: Near the relevant references, say that Figure70 looks at the same wire AB end-on, so the wire appears as a circle; the two sides belong to one thin film and each supplies a pull. Explain that the lower dashed line in Figure69 marks the same wire after moving down, with A'/B' identifying that later position. Connect h to the downward travel without asserting a measured drawing distance. Name the upward film pull and downward F1 in the illustrated setup.
findings.acceptance: Prose connects both diagrams to one apparatus and one wire, distinguishes one film from its two interfaces, and explains the position change using the existing text inventory. No figure/spec/media change or pixel re-review is required to address this text finding.
findings.observationBoundary: Based only on hash-bound spec/inventory/review TEXT. No source image, SVG or preview was opened.

findings.title: Explain the energy distinction without circular technical glosses
evidence: surface free energy, the energy measure relevant to reversible work under these conditions
It should not be equated unconditionally with the change in the whole system's internal energy.
findings.problem: The scientific distinction is correct, but defining surface free energy through reversible work leaves both concepts unexplained. The following sentence adds whole-system internal energy and an ambiguous It. A child has no concrete account of which energy is increasing or why this is not all the energy of the system.
findings.localAction: Lead with the physical change: making more film surface requires energy in this model. Explain reversible here as an ideal slow change that can be undone without energy being wasted by friction/flow resistance, and constant temperature as temperature staying the same. Name the precise surface free-energy measure while retaining U_surface as the textbook model notation. State explicitly that this surface-work measure is not the whole system's internal-energy change; a fixed-temperature process can exchange heat. Replace It with the named surface-work/energy quantity.
findings.acceptance: A child can say what receives the work and why the statement is limited to the stated ideal fixed-temperature process. Do not simplify this into an unconditional claim that work equals total internal-energy gain, or rename the retained U_surface formulas.

findings.title: Ground the local direction and unit explanation in the wire
evidence: Surface tension acts tangentially to the liquid surface
with surface tension coefficient $\sigma$ as the proportionality constant
These are equivalent to joules per square meter
findings.problem: The closing paragraph uses tangentially, local tangent plane, boundary segments and proportionality constant without a concrete gloss. These in the unit sentence points back to units from an unnamed quantity; it never plainly says that sigma, not F, has units N/m. Newtons and joules are not tied to force and energy for this reader.
findings.localAction: Start with the pictured straight wire: the pull runs along the film and at a right angle to AB. Define boundary as the edge where the film meets the wire. Explain the curved-surface rule as using the flat direction of a tiny surface patch at the edge, while preserving the local tangent/boundary condition and vector-direction warning. Explain proportionality as a longer straight contact having a larger pull under the same conditions. Explicitly name sigma's units; briefly gloss newton as a force unit and joule as an energy unit. Retain the exact J/m^2=N m/m^2=N/m relation and the warning against using the whole frame perimeter.
findings.acceptance: The child can identify the relevant edge and force direction, say what sigma measures, and distinguish the force unit from force per unit length. No unit relation, numerical value or curved-boundary qualification changes.
